items.statement: If most people in a group privately disapprove of a practice, it will die out on its own.
items.folk_theory: Disapproval kills norms: a practice nobody likes cannot last.
items.explanation: Pluralistic ignorance keeps disliked norms alive. Each person infers that others approve from the fact that others comply, and that compliance is itself driven by the same inference. The norm is a shared misperception, and it dies only when the private disapproval becomes common knowledge, through a credible published measurement or a visible trendsetter (Bicchieri, The Grammar of Society, ch 5; ledger C44).

items.statement: People will pay out of their own pocket to punish someone who treated them unfairly, even when they will never meet again.
items.folk_theory: People are payoff maximisers: nobody spends money on revenge against a stranger.
items.explanation: Ultimatum-game rejections are robust across decades and countries. In Western student samples about half of offers below a fifth of the pie are rejected (an approximate background figure), and rejection falls sharply when the same low offer is generated by a computer, so what is punished is the inferred intention (Blount 1995). The lab willingness to punish is [E]; what it says about evolution is a separate question (Camerer, Behavioral Game Theory, ch 2; ledger rules 4 and 25).

items.statement: Humans evolved to punish cheats at personal cost, and that evolved trait is what keeps cooperation stable in real communities.
items.folk_theory: Strong reciprocity is settled science and explains real-world cooperation.
items.explanation: Two claims are bundled here. Willingness to pay to punish unfair intentions in the lab is [E]. The claim that this is an evolved trait, strong reciprocity, is contested (Binmore and Shaked 2010; Guala 2012) and is [H] in this course. Field evidence from durable commons shows that real-world sanctioning is mostly cheap, graduated and run by participants, so designs should rest on the cheap version (Gintis, evidence section; Ostrom ch 3; ledger X4, rule 4).

items.statement: Schelling's checkerboard model shows that residential segregation is mainly caused by people's mild preferences rather than by discrimination.
items.folk_theory: Schelling proved that preferences, not discrimination, produce segregation.
items.explanation: The checkerboard is a possibility proof. It shows that mild preferences plus interdependence can produce extreme sorting, and that homogeneity is weak evidence of intolerance. It says nothing about the real-world share due to discrimination, prices, lending or law, and Schelling says so. Real tipping does exist in US census tracts at roughly 5 to 20 percent minority share, higher where measured tolerance is higher (Card, Mas and Rothstein 2008), which is evidence for the dynamic, not for the cause (Schelling ch 4; ledger C29, rule 17).

items.statement: In a stag hunt, if the cooperative outcome pays more for everyone, a group of rational people will reach it.
items.folk_theory: The efficient equilibrium is the rational one, so sensible people find it.
items.explanation: A stag hunt has two equilibria, and which one a population reaches depends on the basin of attraction it starts in, not on how attractive the good outcome is. Under random mixing, best-response updating, large groups and no communication the risk-dominant equilibrium usually has the larger basin and wins; laboratory groups converge to it without communication (Cooper et al.; Van Huyck et al.). Choosing the safe action under uncertainty about the others is defensible, so the failure is structural and so is the fix (Skyrms ch 1; Camerer ch 7; ledger X6, rule 2).

items.statement: Ten minutes of relevant, non-binding talk before a public-goods decision roughly doubles cooperation in the lab.
items.folk_theory: Talk is cheap and therefore empty: only binding commitments change behaviour.
items.explanation: In Dawes, McTavish and Shaklee (1977) relevant discussion raised cooperation from roughly a third to roughly seven in ten (approximate background figures), and communication is the strongest single lever in the Sally 1995 meta-analysis. The promises were unenforceable; talk works by creating the empirical and normative expectations a cooperation norm needs. Expect the effect to decay without sanctions or repetition where defection dominates (Bicchieri ch 4; Gilovich et al. ch 14; ledger rule 12).

items.statement: Tightly knit clusters in a network always slow the spread of a new behaviour.
items.folk_theory: Clusters are bad: insular sub-groups hold new practices back.
items.explanation: Clusters cut both ways. A cluster whose density exceeds one minus the adoption threshold blocks a cascade entering from outside, and by the same arithmetic it protects a behaviour adopted inside it. Costly behaviour is a complex contagion needing several adopting neighbours, so clustered networks spread it faster than random ones (Centola 2010, background). The rule is: seed inside dense clusters and build wide bridges out of them (Easley and Kleinberg ch 19; ledger X7, rule 3).

items.statement: The main structural fact about weak ties is that they tend to be the bridges between groups.
items.folk_theory: Weak ties are about job-hunting: most useful information and jobs come through acquaintances.
items.explanation: The structural claim is robust: by strong triadic closure a local bridge must be a weak tie, and Onnela et al. (2007) confirmed the pattern in phone-network data. The popular job-search claim rests on a small sample, and later work found most jobs arrive through strong or moderately weak ties. Quote the structural claim only, and remember that weak ties carry information, not costly behaviour (Easley and Kleinberg ch 3; ledger C51, rule 33).

items.statement: Willpower is a limited resource that gets used up during the day, so cooperation designs should ration demands on it.
items.folk_theory: Ego depletion: self-control is a muscle that tires.
items.explanation: The registered replication of the ego-depletion effect across 23 labs with N = 2,141 found d = 0.04 with a confidence interval including zero (Hagger et al. 2016, verified), and a later multi-lab effort was similar. The course's replication rule is to build nothing on ego depletion, social priming, power posing, watching eyes, the Stanford Prison Experiment as usually told, groupthink as a syndrome or IAT-based training (Gilovich et al., evidence section; ledger C11, rule 20).

items.statement: Milgram's participants mostly obeyed because they trusted the institution and had no graceful exit, and obedience drops sharply when a peer refuses.
items.folk_theory: Blind obedience: most people are secretly willing to hurt others when told to.
items.explanation: The behaviour replicates: 70 percent continued past 150 volts in Burger's 2009 partial replication (verified) against roughly 82 percent at the same point in Milgram. But obedience fell sharply with victim proximity, an absent authority or a disobedient peer, participants were distressed, and archival work shows engaged followership rather than sadism. The design lesson is exits, peers and legitimacy of refusal, not a verdict on human nature (Gilovich et al. ch 9; ledger C21, rule 22).

items.statement: Repeating an interaction indefinitely solves the prisoner's dilemma.
items.folk_theory: Repetition solves the PD: the shadow of the future guarantees cooperation.
items.explanation: The folk theorem is an existence result. With a long, uncertain and observable future, cooperation becomes one equilibrium among many, including permanent mutual defection. The group must still coordinate on the cooperative equilibrium and detect defection fast enough for retaliation to bite, and under noise it needs forgiving strategies. Repetition permits cooperation; selection is a separate problem (Dixit, Skeath and McAdams ch 10; ledger C27, rule 15).

items.statement: A social norm is whatever most people in the group actually do.
items.folk_theory: Norm equals majority: the norm is what people do.
items.explanation: What most people do is a descriptive norm, sustained by empirical expectations alone and liable to flip when the visible majority changes. A social norm in Bicchieri's sense is a conditional preference that also needs normative expectations, the belief that others think one ought to comply and may sanction, and it can exist while widely violated. The four-way taxonomy (descriptive, convention, social, moral) tells you which lever to pull (Bicchieri ch 1; ledger C42, rule 11).

items.statement: In durable self-governed commons, the first sanction for a rule violation is usually small.
items.folk_theory: Deterrence needs big penalties: make cheating unprofitable from the first offence.
items.explanation: Across Ostrom's long-enduring cases first-offence sanctions are graduated and small. Compliance is quasi-voluntary and contingent on believing that others comply and that violations are likely to be seen, so the first sanction's job is to signal that the rule is alive, to the violator and to everyone watching. Harsh first sanctions drive violations and reports underground and erode the information flow monitoring depends on; escalation is held for repeat offenders (Ostrom ch 3, principle 5; ledger rule 30).

items.statement: Ostrom's eight design principles are conditions found in durable commons, not a set of rules to install.
items.folk_theory: The principles are a recipe: adopt all eight and the commons will hold.
items.explanation: The principles specify no rules; Törbel, the Japanese villages, Valencia and the Philippine zanjeras all run different rules under the same structural conditions. A review of 91 empirical studies (Cox, Arnold and Villamayor-Tomás 2010, verified) found the principles well supported and split three of them, while warning of publication bias and that they capture structure, not processes such as trust and legitimacy. Use them as a diagnostic checklist, and flag scope for digital or knowledge commons (Ostrom ch 3 and evidence section; ledger C47, rule 29).

items.statement: Copying other people is efficient mainly because the people you copy have already filtered out bad options.
items.folk_theory: Copying is lazy: imitation is a cheap shortcut that stops innovation.
items.explanation: In the social-learning tournament (104 entries, Rendell et al. 2010, verified) copying won even when observing cost no less than innovating, because demonstrators perform their best-known action, so what an observer sees is a sample already filtered toward high payoffs. Three caveats travel with the result: it was a computer simulation, not people; the winner discounted stale information; and populations of pure copiers stagnate (Rogers's paradox), so someone must be paid to innovate (Laland ch 3; ledger rule 39).

items.statement: Tipping points are a property of a population's threshold distribution, not of a few influential people.
items.folk_theory: Influencers cause tipping: find the charismatic few and the rest follow.
items.explanation: Schelling's tipping point is an unstable equilibrium in a threshold distribution or adoption curve: below it participation decays, above it snowballs. Whether a cascade can start depends on whether there are enough low-threshold actors and no gap at the low end, so the scarce resource is people who will act when few others have, not charismatic ones. The influencer framing inverts the model (Schelling ch 3; Easley and Kleinberg ch 17; ledger C30, rule 18).
